utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Unless there are matters to be raised before we begin today, there's one matter. I'd like to issue a ruling in private session. Before that -- before that, yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone. Mr. President, we would like to ask that we take a break after the direct examination of the first witness because Dr. Karadzic received some materials late yesterday and some were delivered yesterday after the close of business that he hasn't yet received, and he'd like a chance to review those before beginning his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, I just spoke to the witness this morning and I think that would probably be very good for her as well. She's not feeling well and she asked me if she could have a break after the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much time-frame do we have in mind in speaking about the break? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think our normal 30-minute break would be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Will that suit the witness, Ms. West, as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I would suspect it would be so, but I think probably we could see at the end of the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now the Chamber will issue a ruling on the admissibility of Exhibit D2003, which was marked for identification for the time being. Judge Baird will deliver the Chamber's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: During the cross-examination of the witness Paul Groenewegen, the Defence applied to have admitted into evidence pages 1 and 3 of a Zagreb newspaper article. The article was entitled: "A Single Shot and the Muslim Hits the Ground," and the two pages in question included an interview that the witness had given to the journalist. Ms. West objected to the admission of those two pages on the ground that the witness had testified that he had not used the exact words that appeared in the article. His words had been completely distorted. As a result, the reliability of the article would be called into question because there would have been no certainty that what it conveyed would have been the truth. She contended that although the witness had testified that incident had occurred, it had not occurred in the way it was depicted in the article. The documents would therefore be unreliable unless the journalist came and testified that that was exactly what the witness had said. Mr. Robinson submitted that the witness had acknowledged that he had spoken with the reporter about the topics covered by the article. It will be a matter of weight, therefore, whether what she had reported was exactly what the witness had said or had been distorted in any way. The Chamber considered the arguments of both sides in light of the evidence before the Chamber. The Chamber will now give a compendium of that evidence, pages 22988 to 22991 of the transcript. The accused referred the witness to the article and he quoted what was attributed to the witness by that article at page 3: "From our observation posts, we saw with night-vision equipment the Muslims leave the enclave mainly to smuggle stuff but also to fight. The next day they talked tough about how they cut the Chetniks' throats. These guys were stiff with cocaine. I recognised that, coming from Rotterdam." The accused then asked him what he could have told us about that. It seemed that they had night vision, that they were able to observe nightly excursions of Muslims into Serb territory, and he had heard them brag how they had slipped the Chetniks' throats. The witness gave an answer in double aspect. He first agreed with the accused, stating, "You are entirely right ..." These words are emphasised, and the emphasis is mine. He then went on to add that he had not used those exact words. His words had been distorted. He was then referred to the alleged incident also mentioned in the report concerning the alleged execution of a Muslim soldier by a Serb at page 1, and the accused asked him whether he had really told her that or whether she had made it up. He replied, "Well, of course it is not true that she made it -- she made it up ..." Again, these words are emphasised, and the emphasis is mine. He then ended by stating that as for it having been conveyed in those words, he could not have confirmed. It must be stated that the witness did testify that he did not remember the name of the journalist and that she was reporting from Zagreb, but he certainly had the newspaper report before him and he was in a position to read it, and to all appearances he had, in fact, read it. In answer to the President, he testified that what he told the journalist in respect of the alleged incident that he saw at his observation post corresponded with what he had stated earlier. Also, information about the alleged smuggling and the alleged attack from within to outside the enclave reached them, but he never used the terms reflected in the newspaper. The journalist changed his statement about what they had heard into their actually seeing it. Now, the witness gave evidence that he had not seen the article in a Dutch newspaper, but the article in the Dutch newspaper did not form part of the subject of the application for admission. It will not, therefore, be treated. As the Chamber addressed the evidence, the Chamber was sensible of the fact that at no juncture did the witness dispute that he had given an interview to the journalist and that he had discussed the subject matter of the reports contained in those two pages in that interview. Further, at no stage did the witness repudiate either -- repudiate the report at its core. I emphasise these words, "at its core." In other words, he did not challenge the report when he spoke of the alleged nocturnal excursions by the Muslims and their subsequent vaunting. Neither did he controvert the report when it described the alleged killings of the Muslim by -- of the Muslim soldier by the Serb. As it appears to me -- actually, to the Chamber, the difficulty and concern of the witness resided in the language with which the journalist had clothed the core features -- I emphasise these words - of both those reports. That was the fulcrum of his complaint. En passant, it is instructive to note that at a later stage in his evidence, the witness gave further approval in retrospect of one of the reports in its essence. At page 22996 he was referred to an interview given by Sergeant Batalona in another publication where Sergeant Batalona had commented on the excursions of Muslim fighters and the slaughter of Serbs. The accused then asked him whether this conformed to what he had told the journalist. He replied that a certain similarity was perceptible but he claimed that he had -- he had been told those facts. In the evidential climate existing at page 22988 to 22991, however, the Chamber is disinclined to accept the contention that admissibility of these two pages could only be achieved through the journalist who would be in a position to say exactly what the witness had said. The Chamber is of the opinion that a proper foundation for the admission of the two pages was intrinsic in the evidence of the witness. Accordingly, the need for evidence of the journalist would have been obviated. At the end of the day, when all the evidence in the case has been received, should we get to that point, then it would be a matter for the Chamber to decide what weight it would apportion those two pages. The Chamber will therefore grant the application and admit the two pages into evidence. This is a majority decision, Judge Kwon dissenting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Baird. Shall we bring in the next witness. Ms. West, please call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution calls Mirsada Malagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that you're not tendering any 92 ter associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There are none, Your Honour, and as you know, this was a 92 bis witness that was converted. I was going to ask her a few questions about the Krstic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. We admitted several associated exhibits in that decision, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Malagic. Please make yourself comfortable. Thank you. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is your name?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Mirsada Malagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Right now I live in Vogosca. That's a municipality that belongs to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, can you confirm that you had an opportunity to listen to your testimony in the Krstic case and that testimony accurately reflected what you told the Court?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you were asked about the same issues here in court, would you provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Krstic testimony, as we said, is already admitted. It's P00356. There are no associated exhibits. There had been one outstanding associated exhibit but that has already been admitted through another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to read a short summary. The witness was born in Potocari in 1959. In 1992, she lived in a small village on the Drina River near Bratunac. She lived there with her husband and three sons. She was forced out of her village in May 1992. Between 1992 and 1995, she lived in a number of villages and also in Srebrenica with her immediate family and a number of other extended family members. During that time, she and her family suffered from the deprivations inflicted on the refugees living in the enclave. In particular, there was never enough food to satisfy the needs of the overcrowded city. The witness left for Potocari on July 11th, 1995. Her husband and two eldest sons and brother decided to reach Tuzla by foot through the woods for fear of what would happen to them at the hands of the Bosnian Serbs. Before she left, the witness was injured by shrapnel from Serb shelling of the enclave. The walk to Potocari was difficult for the refugees as they faced constant shelling. The witness was also pregnant at the time. When she arrived at Potocari with her youngest son and father-in-law, the enclave was -- the compound was already full. She found refuge at a factory and remained there until she left Potocari. During the evening of the 12th, she saw many men being taken away and heard screams coming from the houses behind the Zinc factory. On the 13th, she, her son, and her father-in-law were making their way to the buses to be evacuated. Her father-in-law was separated by the BSA. She saw him taken to the yard of the white house where he dropped his bag before proceeding towards the house. The witness and her youngest son were evacuated. She never saw her husband or her two other sons again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, I understand that you don't feel entirely well, and if you need a break, please let us know, but I want to let you know that after I ask you questions, there will then be a break. Ma'am, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 10th of January, 1959, in Potocari, the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in April 1992, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: In April of 1992, I lived in the village of Voljavica, 3 kilometres away from Bratunac. It is right by the Drina River. That's where we had our family house and a farm. I lived there with my husband and my children, that is to say, my three sons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at some point in May were you told to leave your home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who told you to leave your home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 11th of May, the representatives of the Serb people came. That's how they introduced themselves. They were from Pobrdje. Pobrdje was between Voljevci and Srebrenica, and it was the same local commune that Voljevci was. They addressed our people and they said that we had to leave Voljavica, that we could no longer live there, and before that, that we were supposed to come to the local commune in Pobrdje and sign a statement to the effect that we are voluntary leaving our homes and property and that we would never return there again. Then they would evacuate us towards Kladanj by bus because, as they explained it, they could no longer protect us from their paramilitaries. Arkan's men, Seselj's men and other paramilitaries. They did not go into all of that. They said that they could no longer guarantee our safety and security and that's why we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: As result of that information what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, me, my husband and the children, my husband's father and mother and other relatives, as well most of the inhabitants of the village, we decided not to sign any paper to that effect and that we would not surrender and wouldn't come out onto the streets as they demanded so that they would transport us. We simply decided to leave our homes and head for the woods -- or, rather, head for the villages in the direction of Srebrenica. On the evening of the 12th of May, given that we hadn't slept in our homes for the previous twenty or so days, I had gone to my house in early evening to get some clothes and perhaps some covers in order to be able to shelter our kids in case it was cold, and we had no idea how and where we would get to in the end, whether we would be able to get to any village or not. No one really knew that. On that one night, we headed from the village around 8.00, and we arrived after several hours at the first village called Bojici. It was a small village, a hamlet. There was already a large group of people there who had gathered there. Now, as it was dark, we didn't know which way to go further because we didn't know the roads there, and then a local man suggested that he lead us so we would go towards Brezovica, because we were surrounded on all sides by these Serb villages and places where they had already erected their barricades while we were still at our homes. And so at 1.30 a.m., we continued on our journey. All the people who remained and who decided to leave at 3.30, because that had been our agreement earlier that evening, they didn't make it. They didn't have the time. We did manage to get to Brezovica, whereas the others had been attacked. They were surrounded by the Serb soldiers. Whether they were soldiers, reservists, or whatnot, but they were dressed. And they took them to the road from where they evacuated them. I don't know what they did after that with the men. Some of them were killed. I don't know what was the fate of the others, but I reached Brezovica and I stayed there with my in-laws and my husband and my sons. There were a lot of local people from my village there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now we know that you stayed there for about 15 days, but ultimately did you reach Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we couldn't remain there because there was nearby a Serb village, and they explained to us that because of us they, too, would have to leave their village, that they were not safe there on our account. So we decided not to create any problems for them so we decided to leave for Srebrenica. We traveled in the direction of Skenderovici village and then we had to pass by the village of Spat, Sasa. All these villages were in forests, in woodlands. There was also a road there, but we didn't dare take the road because we could be seen, so we felt that it was safer to go through the woods, that that was safer, and we would reach Srebrenica. After some eight hours or so of walking with the children, we arrived close to Srebrenica, in Kula Grad, and then we went to Srebrenica, to downtown Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you entered the downtown area, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: In downtown Srebrenica and on the way there, it was a disaster. That's the only way I can describe the -- what I saw in Srebrenica on that day. It was very smelly. There was the stench of burning. All the houses had been burnt. You would just encounter a stray dog or so. We saw a few people. They had already begun to organise some sort of civilian protection. I don't know what to call it. But anyway, we saw some people as we came to the downtown area itself, and these people tried to organise some kind of welcome for the people who were arriving from all the surrounding villages. For me, that was a more difficult day than the day when I left my home. Perhaps you'll ask me why, but it's hard to describe. I felt miserable, and in fact, I realised then in the -- in that town itself what was in store for us. This was my town. I spent my entire working life or career there. It was -- the city was deserted. It was sad. I saw that we had now we found ourselves in a vicious circle out of which there was no way, and I was wondering what was to come next. There was nowhere to go. The tears just started flowing from my eyes. I couldn't stop it. People asked me why I was crying. I couldn't say. It was really terrible. Srebrenica was disastrous. Everything was so difficult, so sad, so miserable, and as I said, you could smell -- there was the stench of burning. All the houses had been torched.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. I just want to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I just want to clarify a piece of information that you mentioned earlier. You had said on May 12th you had left your village where you had your home, but you also said you hadn't slept in your homes anyways for some period of days before. Was that ten days before or 20 days before?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, after the 17th or 18th of April, I'm not sure, but from that time on -- onwards, we didn't really sleep in our homes anymore. Many things were happening at the time. I can't tell you exactly dates, but at this time many people were taken away. We were in our homes. There were barricades at Pobrdje. In Bjelovac, which was a small place above our village, there were barricades. The mine was occupied, if I can put it that way. It was -- there were people of Serb ethnicity all over there. We were simply prisoners in our own village. We couldn't go to Bratunac anymore. We had nowhere to go. They would pass by in their cars looking for prominent people. These were usually educated people who had degrees, and then they would take them away. There were murders. For instance, one night, outside my home, a car stopped from the direction of Bratunac. Some young men - I assumed that they were trying to escape - were shot at, and on the next day when we returned, across from our house, in Rifeta Malagic's yard, we saw two young men, two dead bodies. Our elders buried them --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Malagic. We now want to focus on the period of time starting in June 1992 when you first arrived in Srebrenica. For those first six to seven months when you arrived, did you live in Potocari, close to Srebrenica, with your brother?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed in Srebrenica just a few days, because my younger son -- or, rather, the middle son fell ill. He had a high fever. We didn't know what to do, because there were no hospitals or medical care, as you know. So we stayed in an apartment which was not far from where I used to work, and then we went to our house. Everything was tumbled. We found some medicines. We found some alcohol, took that with us. That took -- that took about a week, and then I found out that my brothers were still alive, that they were in Potocari. So then we headed for Potocari, where we arrived in June. They had a family home there so we went to that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we know that you stayed there for about six or seven months and ultimately left. What made you leave Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: For those seven months that we spent in Potocari, it was difficult. It was disastrous, in fact. You were happy every single day that you were still alive. Every single day there was shelling. You would go to get some water and you would be shelled. They were so close that they could actually see you with the bare eye -- with the naked eye. They were in positions very close by. They could see whatever was happening in Potocari. So we had difficulty. Nothing was functioning anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did something happened to your brother's house that made you leave?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Many shells actually fell on my brother's house, but they were smaller calibre shells. So we moved from room to room. We ended up in the garage of the house, trying to find shelter from the shells. Until one day somebody said it was a guided missile. The house was hit, and fortunately on that day, my brother, my husband and my elder son were away. They had gone to Zepa to try and get some food, and by some lucky coincidence I was next door. I wasn't in the house itself. I heard a large explosion. Everything was trembling and shaking. And then when the smoke dissipated, we saw that the house was no more. It was razed to the ground, and it was impossible to live there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you just --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: That was the reason --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You just mentioned food. Can you describe for us the food situation in Srebrenica and Potocari during the winter of 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, those of us who had left our homes in May, we were -- we had food shortages from day one. There was nothing to eat. So my husband and my elder son and a few other young men had to try and go back to our house in Voljavica through the woods, risking their lives to see if they could find something to eat. The agony continued in Potocari. There was this huge number of people coming down from Bjelavica and other areas and tried to get the food that was left behind in the barns and so on. There was some corn left there and some grain and so on. So that is how we managed to actually feed ourselves. However, it went on like that until the first snow fell. When the snow fell in 1992, then it became really critical. There was nothing to get from anywhere else. There was no food. All of the barns had been emptied by that time, because in Srebrenica there were a lot of people who had come from Zepa and the Han Pijesak municipality. They were all there. So that food was getting scarcer and scarcer. And if we had something to trade we would in order to get food, but even those people who were from Srebrenica itself, toward the end of December and January, they, too, had been left without any food. So our villages from the Drina valley area were now hungry. There was famine. In January, February, there was barely anything. Then we would go from home to home and -- well, we started begging practically. We had to feed our children. The men, my husband and my older son, my brother, they would venture out and walk kilometres, tens of kilometres to find something, but sometimes they would return without finding anything and they would come back home hungry. I tried to obtain whatever I could from people I knew, from friends. They would help. And I would mostly use that food to feed the kids. And it wasn't really even enough to -- to feed them. It was just survival. It was --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. And as a result of giving the food to the children, was there much left for you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. I never even thought about myself. I always -- my first thoughts were always for the kids. I would always give them the food first, and then if there was nothing left after they ate, then there was nothing that I would eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In January of 1993, did you become ill? And did you speak --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- to a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a doctor in Srebrenica. He happened to remain in Srebrenica because he had a father and mother there. He didn't want to leave them, but he was a doctor from the centre for -- a medical centre, and my husband went to see him. I could barely walk. I -- they took me there. They helped me there. And when he examined me, he asked me, "Mirsada, what can I give you? You are hungry. You're malnourished, and you need food. You don't need medicines. The only thing that I -- that you need now would be food, because no medication that I have would help you. If you can manage at least a cup of coffee every day to raise your blood pressure," which was at that time -- "which is so low, that way you could survive." So he proposed, he said that there was some kind of vitamin cocktail injection. He said that they would give this injection to me intravenously and try to pull me back from the dead, as it were. And so every day I was given these shots. He had a lot of difficulty to find a vein where he could actually administer the injection, because my body was -- my tissue was dying out. So after five injections that I received every morning - I think this was the 7th or 8th of January - at 9.00 in the morning I received a shot and then later that day we were bombed. The aeroplanes bombed the village and this doctor was killed. This only doctor that was left there was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, in regard to his comments about coffee, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I told the people in the house about this. Now, in -- this house was full of refugees. There were families in each room, different families, and one of the people there told me that there was a woman who had shop and who had some stores of food that she had earlier buried somewhere and that I should go and talk to her, that she had coffee, and I went and asked her, and she asked for gold. I gave her what I had, a handful of jewellery or something, and I asked this man to go and see if he could get something from this woman. This man went with my gold. This woman then in exchange sent some coffee, 100 grams of coffee and a little bit of sugar to use with the coffee, and she also sent a litre of juice, fruit juice. Blueberry juice.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What did you do with the juice?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, this juice, you know, if you're starving and your kids had not seen any kind of juice for months, I just could not drink the juice. I made coffee for myself, and as for the kids, I made some juice with -- for them. And for a few days they could use this bottle of juice, mix it with water and then use it for a couple of days. Now, on the next day, my youngest son, Adnan, came to me and said, "Mummy, are you hurting?" And I said, "No, my son. Why are you asking?" And he said, "Well -- [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ma'am, just a second. I don't think we're getting any interpretation. Could you repeat your answer starting with those words that you said to your son, "Why are you asking?" And start from there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I asked him, "Why are you asking, son?" He said, "Well, shall I make a glass of juice for you with water?" And then I said that he should go on and do it because he knew that I couldn't drink this up, that I wouldn't, that he would drink it up. And then when he did prepare it for me, then I told him to drink it up myself because I just didn't have the heart to do it while he would just watch me drinking this juice. He was eight years old. It was difficult. I'll never forget those days of my life ever. It is true that people died of starvation, because there was nothing anymore that you could find under this snow cover. You were lucky if you survived from one day to the next.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you now about the international food convoys during those years and the food that was brought in. Can you tell us in 1993 whether Srebrenica received food from any international groups?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: In the first months of 1993, very early on there was an operation. There were parachutes. There were air-lifts, as it were, and then there were convoys, and in February, sometime in February 1993, in Srebrenica, I can't really recall because we were so weak, you know, nothing functioned. We had no calendars, no watches. Nothing really worked. But I know when the air-lift began, when they started dropping this food from aeroplanes, that people managed to survive on those rations, and the food was distributed every day. And we were assisted significantly by the refugees from Konjevic Polje because they had some food with them. I exchanged -- I had some -- I had nothing to exchange, so then they just lent me some food. They gave me some flour and some other foodstuffs, and I made some kind of bread or cake or something of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's move to 1994. Can you describe the amount of food that came into Srebrenica during that year.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, when the convoys began arriving in Srebrenica, very early on, there was a lot of food arriving. It was relatively sufficient. You would get 1 to 2 kilos of flour per family, per family member, some sugar which was measured in grams, some oil, cooking oil. So early on, at the very start, there was enough. We didn't have enough salt or sugar. That was always measured in grams. You would get one of the jar lid -- jar lids of -- of sugar or salt, that was it. Sometimes there was rice, but then we would have no salt to use it with the rice. So that's how it went on. But we had flour, so the people who had already suffered so much were happy to have bread at least. Now, in 1994, everything was tilled in Srebrenica, every inch of the ground, because people tried to sow as much as they could to survive. I started going to Potocari, where I started a vegetable garden, because we received some seeds from the humanitarian aid organisations. We got some carrot seeds and other seeds, so we planted that. Now, in 1994, in the first half and up until the fall, the situation was bearable as far as food was concerned. There was no shooting -- not as much shooting, so it was possible to work the land.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So what happened --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: So there was some food.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What happened in the winter of 1995 and the spring of 1995? What was the food situation then?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, already that winter the amounts of food diminished, and the convoys did not arrive that often anymore, and when they did, they brought a lot less food. For instance, in the beginning there were would be 13, 14 trucks of humanitarian aid, and later on the number of trucks was halved. There would be five or six. I tried when the trucks unloaded at the former department store in Srebrenica. A truck would come and you would think that a lot of humanitarian aid had arrived, but when they lift the tarpaulin, you would see just one line of sacks, flour and salt trampled with soldiers' boots. That means that somebody had walked over them and taken a lot, because the trucks had not set off towards Srebrenica half empty. That means that the humanitarian aid was unloaded first somewhere else. And it was just for the sake of appearances that something was left at all, that the world would see or be given to see that some trucks had arrived in Srebrenica. And that very winter we started our trips looking for food again. We went mainly towards Zepa. My brothers, my husband went to Zepa because I had a sister there, and she and her family had a bit more food. I don't know how. And she let us know that we could come and she would give us some flour. My eldest son went on those journeys, too, and we tried to stretch whatever food we had for as long as we could so that we would have at least one meal a day, which was not very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, we're going to start talking about July of 1995, but before we do, can you first describe for us the number of people who were crowded into Srebrenica in June and July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in July 1995, in fact towards the end of June and the beginning of July, I don't know how many people there were exactly, but it was a huge mass of people on a small area. The figure that I heard - I don't know if its true - was 40.000 people over 50 square kilometres. In every room in every flat there was one family. Every house was full, every garage, every shed. Every schoolhouse with improvised classrooms were used to put up these refugees, people who had nowhere else to go --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So after -- pardon me for interrupting. But after the attack began on the 6th of July, did more people come to the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that, even the refugees who had earlier been in Zeleni Jadar started going down towards Srebrenica. There were little wooden houses there housing a lot of people, perhaps up to 3.000. And when the shelling started, when the first UNPROFOR observation post, I think it was called the Ljubisevic [phoen], near Zeleni Jadar, was attacked those people started retreating towards the town itself, towards Srebrenica. They did not feel safe up there anymore because the Serb forces were advancing and these people started going towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when the shelling began in earnest on the first day, July 6th, where were you when you first heard it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: On that day I was going from Potocari to Srebrenica and I was halfway when I heard the first shells exploding. The detonations could be heard in Srebrenica. When I heard them, my legs buckled. I don't know how I managed to reach Srebrenica. It was so horrible after that lull, after that relatively quiet spell. I saw again the images of chaos, shelling, killing, and I don't know how my legs carried me to Srebrenica where I went to see what was going on because my husband and children were trying to do something around our garden.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in the course of the 6th, the 7th, the 8th, did the shelling continue at the same pace? Did it increase? Did it decrease?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: During those days the shelling continued. As I explained earlier, Srebrenica was packed. There were so many people. Every shell found its target. It did not have to be precise, because it simply couldn't miss. It just had to hit Srebrenica and it would kill somebody. People were lining up for water. Some were working their vegetable gardens. The hospital was full again because people were getting killed and wounded. You were nowhere safe anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: During those days, did you see any wounded people or any dead people on the streets?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. One of those days a woman physician by the name of Fatima, I don't know her last name, was wounded when she was walking from the hospital to her apartment in our building. Also close to our house my husband's uncle was seriously wounded when a shell fell into his garden. And there were many other people who were injured while queueing for water, because you needed water for the bathroom, because we had to keep up our hygiene. We had no water for the toilet. There were only improvised toilets outside. And the children had to venture outside frequently because they had to get firewood as we had no electricity for a long time, and the woods around Srebrenica were already all used up and you had to go further and further to get firewood. All the way up to the 10th of July, the hospital was already completely full. That speaks eloquently about how many people were wounded and how many were in danger.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's talk now about the evening of the 10th of July. On that evening, did you have a meeting, a family meeting with all the members of your immediate family and extended family?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, that afternoon, around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m., I'm not sure, a huge column of people started moving towards the UNPROFOR base on the 10th of July, and we left the town too. We were told we should go towards the UNPROFOR compound several kilometres away from [Realtime transcript read in error "Vienna"] Srebrenica in the direction of Potocari, and I with my children headed there to see what to do next, but when we got to the gate, there was again a huge mass of people, and we were told to return. UNPROFOR soldiers told us to go back to our homes, that we were safe, that they would protect us from the Serb forces, that we need not panic --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's just stop there for a moment. When you talk about this UNPROFOR compound, are you speaking about the one that's closer to Srebrenica, or are you speaking about the one that's further away in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: The one that's closer to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And that evening, what was the discussion that you had with your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: We had all returned to our apartments where we were housed, but a lot of people were coming in from Zeleni Jadar and the area of Srebrenica called Ucina Basta. Everybody was fleeing closer to the UN force. Every building, every entranceway was full of people. The women had brought some flour to be able to make bread, at least for the children. At any rate, that night nobody slept. My husband, his brothers, his parents, myself, did not know exactly what was going on, but we were talking and we made a decision, a decision for ourselves, as many others probably did, that I, my youngest son and my father-in-law should go to the UNPROFOR compound if the Serb soldiers occupied the town whereas the rest of them would go through the woods towards Tuzla. They did not trust the Serb forces to treat them well if they are captured. They thought that the Serbs would not do any harm to the women and children but that they should try to get to the free territory through the woods, and that's how the night passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you want to leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, things being what they were during those days, everybody wanted not to leave Srebrenica for the sake of leaving but because they felt unsafe because of the chaos that reigned, because of their fear from the Serb forces that were advancing, and they had already taken one check-point held by the UNPROFOR. Other UN observation posts were not safe either. The circle around the town was getting tighter and tighter, and the Serb troops were closer and closer. And out of fear, everyone wanted to leave that night because they did not feel safe anymore. They feared for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to move to the next day to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one second. I wonder whether you can scroll back the transcript. Line 20 of the previous page, this is what is reflected in the transcript: "We were told we should go towards the UNPROFOR compound several kilometres away from Vienna in the direction of Potocari." I take Vienna to be Srebrenica. Is it correct, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Srebrenica, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's move to July 11th, in the morning hours, after you and your family have left the apartment. To where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: My family and I and everyone else who lived in that building and in the buildings around us, everybody headed towards Potocari, the UNPROFOR compound. And we didn't know where we would go on next. Maybe Potocari, but for that moment we were going towards the UNPROFOR compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At some point before you started going to Potocari, were you separated from your husband, your brothers, and your two oldest sons?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Where --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: In peacetime it used to be a petrol station just before the gates of the UNPROFOR compound. We reached that point when we saw a doctor going down the street, through the crowd, and asking the young men to return, some of them, to the hospital to put the wounded on the trucks because the hospital was full of wounded people. At that moment, shells started falling into the crowd, and it was a huge mass of people with many children there. The children started screaming. There was complete chaos. Nobody could control it anymore. And as we had agreed earlier, my father-in-law, my youngest son and myself headed towards the UNPROFOR compound, whereas my brothers, my husband, my eldest son, and the son of my in-laws headed left of the petrol station towards Susnjari. We didn't even have time to say good-bye. We just followed our earlier agreement, and we didn't even say good-bye. When we got to about 50 metres away from the UNPROFOR compound, the shells were still falling. And in that chaos, nobody knew where anybody else was. People were falling from the explosions, from the shrapnel, some from fear. The heat was insufferable. Some people were just fainting right outside the gate of the UNPROFOR compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you yourself suffer an injury?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: One shell fell across the wire fence that surrounded the compound, and one shell fell opposite us on a hard surface, on concrete. All of us fell to the ground. That's how close we were. I thought my son and my father-in-law were killed because nobody was getting up for the longest time. And after a while, those who were not injured started getting on their feet. My son was so pale, white as a sheet, and he looked terrible, as did my father-in-law, but they were not injured. I myself was. I was wounded in my right shoulder blade, and I was bleeding. My son got very frightened at the sight of blood. And I took my kerchief off my head. I was wearing it to protect myself from the sun, and perhaps that kerchief saved my life at the time, because there was a lot of shrapnel in the black -- in the back of my kerchief, and a lot of shrapnel got caught in that kerchief and in the jumper I was wearing. The shrapnel that got to my shoulder blade was stopped by the top of my jumper and remained there. The wound itself was an entry and exit wound. There was no embedded shrapnel in me. And when the shelling stopped, chaos continued. People were going in and out of the UNPROFOR compound. They didn't know what to do. Nobody knew what was going on. It was complete chaos. Crying, screaming, panic, commotion. It's very hard to describe what was going.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, at some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you clarify with the witness which UN compound we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you speak of this compound, is this the compound near Srebrenica, Bravo Company, or is this the compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: The one closer to Srebrenica still.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At some point thereafter did the crowd begin to move towards the UN compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And -- and the distance between the Bravo Company UN compound Srebrenica and the Potocari compound, it's about 4 kilometres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you move along with the crowd?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Why did you leave? Why did you move to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, after staying for several hours in that UNPROFOR compound and in the street, we heard the sound of aeroplanes at some point, and the soldiers of UNPROFOR, who were on an APC, were unable to communicate with us. We didn't understand each other, but they motioned towards the sky, the aeroplanes, and we understood that these planes would be bombing Serb positions around. And they also showed us that we should go to Potocari, all of us. And the mass of people obeyed. Some people started first and, as it goes with large crowds, others followed, and that's how we all took the real asphalt road that leads to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, as you walked, as we understand it was with your younger son and your father-in-law with you, did you carry any bags?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, because when I got wounded, I did not feel my right arm anymore. I was unable to carry my bag. My priority was my son. I held his hand with my left hand, and I forgot about the bag. I left it where it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened on this 4 kilometre walk as you went to the compound.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of our journey from the base, at the very outset when we were still hearing those planes I mentioned, close to the football pitch by the compound we could still hear the planes, but they were farther and farther as we walked. They must have been close to Zalazje. I know that area. We heard several explosions and continued on our way. In the beginning it was a disorganised crowd, but in a while a column formed, because of course people walked at a different pace. They were elderly people and children who couldn't walk fast, and the women had to stay with the children. At any rate, a column formed over a stretch of the road, and the shells were falling all the time on both sides of the road. I can't say they were hitting the road itself and the crowd, at least not where I was, but they were falling close to the road on both sides. Some people were wounded not so seriously. They were able to go on walking. A few people were killed. But really, believe me when I say that nobody was able to carry or help anyone else. You were only concerned about getting out of there alive. You didn't know whether you yourself would make it to Potocari. A woman got killed close to me. She was just covered with a blanket and left by the side of the road. There was nobody around me that I knew at the time, only my youngest son and my father-in-law. And we went on for about a kilometre and a half outside Potocari when two UNPROFOR trucks caught up with us. The trucks were traveling slowly, so they could see everything very well, and they couldn't drive fast through the crowd. But the people made way for the trucks, so they were able to go faster than the people. And the tarpaulins of the trucks were torn. So I saw my eldest son and a friend of his on one of the trucks. This other boy was my son's close friend in Srebrenica. I was surprised to see him on that truck, but he saw me, too, and raised his hand in recognition. And then the trucks drove on. That was not far from the Potocari UNPROFOR compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's talk about what happened when you arrived at the Potocari compound. Were you able to get into -- inside the UN base itself, inside the fence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, on the barricade itself, it wasn't really a barricade. We called it that. That was a band that was put up there by the UNPROFOR soldiers. They had an interpreter there who explained to us that we who were arriving could not stay at the base that was already brimming with people. There was no room for anybody else. So we should look for a place elsewhere. There was a complex of factories there. There was the factory of the 11th of March where I worked just before the war, then the transport company, the Feros company and so on. So these areas in front of the factories were where people had to stay because as they were arriving they had nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were you able to get inside one of the factories?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, again with my son and my father-in-law, I managed to get back to one of the factories. At that first gate I managed to get in. My son was very frightened. I was wounded, and I thought somehow that we'd be safer if we were indoors. How do I explain this? Although that room did not have any windows or anything. These were former offices. When I got in there were other women and children there, elderly men, then other women who were without children. They were standing within the compound of that factory. It was important at least to find shelter for the children so that they would not spend that night out in the open. So I spent the night there with my son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, I'm noting the time. How much longer would you need? Shall we take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think that would be an idea, but if I can ask for the Court's indulgence. I know this witness would like to have a break at the end of the direct as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So why don't we take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, ma'am, we're going to take a break for about half an hour. We'll resume probably about five past 11.00. You now may be -- you may now be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, there's another matter I would like to deal with in private session. Yes, you may be excused, Madam Malagic. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber found the site visit to Sarajevo to be invaluable and was greatly assisted by it. It is therefore considering organising a site visit to locations in Srebrenica. At this stage, and due to the number of municipalities covered in the indictment and the different nature of allegations in relation thereto, the Chamber is not presently envisaging visiting locations in the municipalities but would like to hear from the parties on this issue as well. As was done with the previous visit, I would therefore ask that parties file submissions addressing the following matters: 1) whether a visit to the municipalities covered in the indictment would be beneficial; 2) to identify the proposed locations to be included in the site visit and a preliminary itinerary of the same; 3) to identify the participants in the visit; and, 4) any other relevant matters. The Chamber asks that these submissions be filed confidentially no later than Tuesday, 31st of January, 2012.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After this break would the Defence need another break after the conclusion of her testimony in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 10 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, when, we stopped earlier, we were discussing the fact that you and your son went into one of the factories on the 11th. When you were inside the factory, where was your father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, my father-in-law was within the same factory compound except that he was outside the factory. Actually, we were divided by this window that wasn't really there. There wasn't any glass or anything. It was on the ground floor. We could communicate except for the fact that we were indoors and he was outside within the factory compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is during the day of July 11th. Can you tell us whether anything noteworthy happened during the night of July 11th while you were in the factory?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that night of the 11th of July while we were in the factory was peaceful. We can put it that way. There were short bursts of gunfire that could be heard somewhere around us, but it wasn't really within the compound where I was. In the early evening shells fell, but not into Potocari. But - how do I put this? - above Djogazi, the village of Djogazi, below Caus, at the location of Likari where the separation lines were basically, where UNPROFOR used to be stationed. At any rate, that is where shelling was heard from, and that is the only thing that was memorable as far as the early evening of the 11th of July is concerned, but the night itself was peaceful until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the next morning, so that would be the morning of July 12th. During that morning and into the afternoon, did you see any Bosnian Serb soldiers mingling with the crowds?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, at first in the morning, I don't know exactly when, it was 9.00 or 10.00, I think, from the direction of Djogazi and Peciste, this other village up there, that is what I could see. I mean, that's the first time I saw these Serb soldiers because old houses were on fire, haystacks and some straw as well as some sheaves of wheat. They were getting closer and closer to the centre of Potocari itself. After that they were firing again. This was celebratory gunfire. We knew that these were Serb soldiers as they were getting closer to us, and then they started mingling with the people. At the moment -- or, rather, at the compound where I was, they were walking around. They were asking people where our soldiers were, where our houses were, where our children were, where our sons were, questions like that. What we decided to do now. Do we know what lay in store for us. One soldier said quite literally to me and a woman who was next to me -- actually he walked into this room, he was a neighbour of hers and they knew each other well, he said, Go to Tuzla. You will be evacuated probably in the direction of Tuzla, and be sure that you're going to see a scenario like this one over there soon too. So, in the morning hours and around midday, they were walking around asking people questions. At that point in time they didn't really touch anyone, if you will, until the afternoon. In the afternoon they started taking groups of men out. They were questioning them. They were taking them out to these houses that were behind factory. There were private houses there, too, and also there was a cornfield. There was a metal plaque there. It was taken from the fence. And before that, on the 11th of July, we went to get water from there. There were toilets there. We took children to the toilet and so on. However, on the 12th of July, in the afternoon, I went out there again to take my son to the toilet, and I was worried. I was deep in my own thoughts, and I didn't really look carefully, and as I got to that fence, perhaps only a few metres away, I saw soldiers all of a sudden who stood there in the area that we were passing by. These soldiers did not say anything to me. One of them simply waved his hand, showing me that I should move away. Only Serb soldiers were there who were in uniform for the most part. There weren't any of our people there in these houses. Of course, they would not allow people to pass by those houses. I went back to where I had set out from, and I didn't go there again. So during that entire early evening they were taking groups of men out, and they were being questioned. That's what I could see in front of the compound. Efendic was questioned, for instance, Hamed. And then he was take away. And then Salihovic Ahmo. He was also taken out. And then the son of a colleague of mine was taken out. She brought him to Potocari. He was questioned twice, and the third time they took him out he was never returned again. For the most part, these people who they took out were never returned, these people who were taken out towards these houses out of these masses of people, but they were never returned again. That is when that night fell too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, on that evening did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. No. There was no chance of sleep that night. I hadn't slept the previous night either. I just sat there, and that night as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, by the morning of the 13th, the following day, what was your state of mind? What did you want to do? Did you want to stay or leave?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, after surviving that kind of night in Potocari, I, and I think all others, wanted to get to this UNPROFOR barricade, as we called it a moment ago, to enter that area and to be evacuated as we had been promised earlier on. The promise was that everybody would be evacuated. I was informed in the early evening of the 12th that the first buses or trucks, I'm not sure, had already taken some people -- or, rather, women. First women with babies. That is what they said. And then all of us all of a sudden wanted to leave and to get to these buses as soon as possible, these trucks, to leave this compound, this chaotic situation that we were in with our children. The temperature was high. There wasn't any food. It was very hard for the children. There was no milk for the children. Nothing could keep in that kind of temperature. Because of this fear during that night, everyone wanted to leave as soon as possible. And everyone wanted to leave at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's talk about your leaving Potocari on the 13th. At some point did you, your youngest son, and your father-in-law walk towards the buses?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And once you got past what you called the barricade or the red ribbon did you see the buses?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In which direction were they facing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: All the buses and trucks were facing Bratunac. They were parked facing Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: As you -- as you approached the buses, was your father-in-law walking next to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. But before the buses, as we were walking towards the buses, at that moment, from Bratunac a vehicle arrived. Perhaps I'm not going to describe it properly, I don't know. It looked like a jeep to me. It was open. It didn't have a roof. These Serb soldiers were armed, were in that vehicle, and among them there was an old man. I knew that man. All the other locals knew him too. My father-in-law knew him in particular, because they worked together at Sase Srebrenica, the Zinc mine. This was Ilija Petrovic. He was insulting us, cursing us, swearing at us, cursing our Balija mothers. He said, "Now go to your Alija, you'll fare a lot better. Had you listened to Babo, you would not be living through everything that you've been living through." A lot of insults. At that time my father-in-law just said to me: "Now we're certainly done in." He probably wanted to say that we'd never see each other again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What happened to your father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: After that vehicle passed, there were Serb soldiers standing again who were separating men from us women. Women and children went to the right-hand side towards the buses, to the right of the buses, and all the men were being taken to the left. That is when they took my father-in-law and also my sister's husband, then other relatives, many relatives who were nearby and who had passed this barricade together with us. I know all of them. And for the most part they took them to this white house, as they called it. However, as we were walking towards the buses, as soon as this bridge was passed - how do I put it? - in the yard they had to discard their bags. I saw my father-in-law throw away his bag, that's what the orders were, and then they walked towards the house without anything. We went on towards the bus and then we could no longer see from the buses. Now, whether they went to the house or above the house, what happened to these people after that we could no longer see.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, have you ever seen your father-in-law again?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you successfully get on a bus with your son?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was your sister on the same bus?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mrs. Malagic, when was the last time you saw your husband, Salko?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, as for my husband as well as my children, I last saw them when we parted in Srebrenica, as I said a moment ago, in front of the UNPROFOR compound when we went our separate ways. I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how old was your husband at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, 44, I think. He was 44 years old. Forty-four, 45 --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, at some point --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: -- almost.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. At some point in recent years did you receive notice that his remains had been recovered?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When did you get that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the beginning of June 2009. 2009 I received notification concerning my husband first. That was somehow just before the funerals. So I just went there for the identification process, and I had to sign these papers and so on. Four months after that I received another summons from Tuzla to go and identify my younger son, which I did. So we had these memorial services for both of -- for both my husband and son and they were both buried at the memorial centre in Potocari. My father-in-law was buried a few years before that. I don't know exactly. And a week before I received this information concerning my arrival in The Hague, I was called from Tuzla. I was told to come for notification again, that -- namely, that my older son had been found too. I haven't done that yet. I decided to take care of this in The Hague first because I didn't know how would I feel after all of this torment that I would go through in Tuzla again. It is not easy to go through that kind of thing there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, in regard to your middle son Admir, the one you indicated that you had last seen at Srebrenica, how old was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: When Srebrenica fell, he was 15 years old and 5 months.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the older son that you just mentioned that you very recently received the notification that his remains have been recovered, how old when you -- was he when you saw him for the last time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: He was about six years older than this other son. So my eldest was about 20 years old. He was five years older, five to six years older than Admir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And your youngest son, your surviving son, the one who was with you in Potocari, how old was he then when you were in the Potocari compound?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: He was 10 at the time, turning on 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And where does he live now?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: My son lives in Vogosca now as I do. We're both renting a place. We're waiting to get more permanent housing. There's a building that is supposed to be completed. The construction is supposed to be completed in June. And he's married. He has a son, and they live in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When Srebrenica was shelled in July 1995 and you made your way to Potocari, you were pregnant; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When did you give birth?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: My daughter was born on the 21st of January, 1996. So the other day she turned 16 while I was here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what was the condition of her health when she was born?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, all the problems and all the torment that I went through throughout my pregnancy and the horrors in Srebrenica that we went through left a mark on my daughter so that when she was born, she was not a healthy baby. We spent a lot of time in hospital in Tuzla. She also had problems with her hips. While they were treating one hip, the other hip turned bad and there were complications. So then we ended up in Sarajevo. I took her everywhere, seen all the doctors, but she had to undergo surgery so that she had three operations on the right hip. We spent up to three and a half months in hospital, and then it would be followed by six months of rehabilitation, and then on one occasion she was infected. She -- she got an infection after the surgery, and she barely survived, but thanks to the doctors and my efforts, I managed to save her and bring her up so that she's not a handicapped person today, but she is under constant medical control. She would undergo physical therapy in the winter and then during the summer vacation she would also have to go to a spa for rehabilitation. All of this as recommended by the doctors who treated her. So right now her condition is relatively good. She attends school, but she cannot do physical education because she is a handicapped person in a way, so she has to take these exams, these subjects, she has to take them theoretically in order to receive a grade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, ma'am, do you still own your home on the Drina River near Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How often do you go back there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in the summertime frequently. Last year I went on many occasions, but I don't go on a regular basis. Whenever I feel homesick I go there. And then I go to the memorial centre, and on those occasions I also go to our house. But one of the reasons why I avoid going there more frequently is that the memories are very painful. When I walk into the house, it's really painful. I did patch up the house so that I can spend the night there if I need to, a day or two or five, for as long as I can stay there, but I cannot really take it mentally, because when I go there on my own, my entire life I see before my -- me, and then it's really difficult. So what I do is basically I just go to the house, enter, walk around it and then leave. It's just difficult. I can't bear to be there on my own. The memories of my children, my husband, the life that I had before 1992, all of that weighs heavily on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Malagic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I wonder if we might inquire whether the witness is feeling okay to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Malagic, your testimony in previous case which you gave 12 years ago was admitted in lieu of your examination-in-chief in this case as well, and in addition to further questions asked by Ms. West, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Karadzic, but before that would you like to take a break? Otherwise, we'll take break at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can wait for the regular break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good morning. I wish good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, to you, Ms. Malagic.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to express my solidarity for your loss and the suffering that you went through, and my gratitude for agreeing to see my assistant who interviewed you. And in view of what you have gone through, I would rather not put any questions to you. However, your statement is rather broad and there are just several things that I would appreciate it if you could help us to clarify them and get a full picture. So I do have to put some questions to you. Now, first of all, is it correct that the crisis in your village, Voljavica, began sometime after the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: In my village, even before the 12th of May, the crisis was in -- the crisis was there, but I don't know what happened because I left Voljavica on the 12th of May already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. That is the year that Ms. West began questioning the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 8th of May the Green Berets and the Patriotic League -- or, rather, the Muslim fighters, killed Judge Zekic near Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question, because at the time I was in Voljavica, and the event that you are describing, according to what people said, was in the area between Potocari and Srebrenica, and at the time I really did not have any information as to what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you don't need to have this information, but that's why I'd like to clarify this to have a full picture.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: One evening, not far from my house we saw a column going from Bratunac, a column of vehicles. It didn't take very long. I don't know how much time it took. And then it went back to Bratunac. We didn't know what this was all about, but we heard from a man who lived in Pobrdje and whose house was in the vicinity of some houses of Serbs because there were both Serb and Muslim houses in that village. So we heard stories from him that he learned that Zekic was killed there, that he was in that column, and that he was -- that, in fact, it was him who was being taken in that column for his funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. So you saw this funeral convoy, but did you hear that when he was killed that he was driving in his own private vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know -- you mentioned Hranca, Hranca is the outskirts of Bratunac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Novi Sad Corps that you mention in your various statements was deployed there as regular JNA forces and that it began its withdrawal towards Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. If you allow me to explain this, I know where Hranca is, and I also know that the Novi Sad Corps was stationed in Bratunac at the time, Mr. Karadzic, and at that time, Mr. Karadzic, the work obligation was declared in Bratunac. My sister-in-law worked in a company there, and for six days she went to work, and she experienced this. She met these troops, and we heard that they were from the Novi Sad Corps, and I consider, it's my opinion, that up until that time there had never been any troops in Bratunac or in that area overall. My brother, my husband, my relatives, they all served their military service in Belgrade, Novi Sad, in Serbia and in other parts of the country. So there were no regular troops in that area up until then. Now, why they had come then, I really don't know. I don't think that they were trying to defend us, because had they done that, we wouldn't have gone through what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in your statements you confirmed, didn't you, that you had been told that the JNA was in Bosnia in order to separate the fighting Muslims and Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that these Novi Sad Corps units had come from Central Bosnia and that they were on their way to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure of their journey. I cannot see how Novi Sad Corps could be from Central Bosnia and then be withdrawing towards Yugoslavia and towards Novi Sad. I cannot really answer that question. Now, where they had come to Bratunac from, I really don't know, because I was in Voljavica, in my village. But the first explanation, the first thing that we were told by your own people, by Serbs, was that this was the corps that was allegedly there to keep the peace in Bratunac. But we weren't even able to go to Bratunac anymore, so what kind of peace they were trying to keep there I really don't know, and I wonder who it is that they were supposed to protect in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just clarify one thing? Would you agree that the fact that the corps had its headquarters in Novi Sad, that the JNA had as its area of responsibility the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia? So the Novi Sad Corps would not stay in Novi Sad alone. It would be deployed as necessary, as required.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is not the witness for this type of question. She is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. West. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
