utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Hranca this convoy that was headed for Yugoslavia, this convoy was attacked and some soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was on the 3rd or the 4th of May, and you never heard that there was an attack on a convoy that was moving and that -- that was not in combat deployment? You didn't hear of that withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Voljavica have their own units or was it demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Voljavica did not have any units of its own, that's for sure. I don't know exactly what the date was, but your forces, your representatives from Bratunac, came one day, one morning, and they issued an ultimatum. They said if anybody had any weapons that they should surrender them, and at their head was a police officer. He was a police officer in peacetime. I knew him. His name was Miladin. I was really surprised to see him there. But in any case, he was there with a number of soldiers, and they came to the school, and they said that we should inform everyone that they should surrender their weapons. And on that day, everyone, all those people who had weapons for which they had permits, they -- they surrendered them. So that Voljavica did not have a unit, nor could it defend itself. It didn't have anything to do it with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Ekrem Malagic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was conferred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- awarded a golden lily posthumously?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, please put a pause.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think the witness answered the question by saying no. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you didn't know that he was posthumously awarded the highest wartime -- well, because the way we form negative sentences and the way it's done in English, because that's different, your answer was no, you didn't know; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Osman Malagic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that he was a prominent military commander of one of the units of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is this: This brother-in-law of mine was killed at the very beginning, early on, and I don't know when he could have become such a great commander. I don't think he had enough time. All he had was this big desire, which he did, and he had a group of young men with him and they were going to their own house on the Drina River. That's where they were headed. They didn't have any weapons with them. Now, if they had any kind of contraptions or anything that was sort of improvised, I don't know, but I know that he was killed on that day on his way to his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Osman Malagic was killed on the 12th of June [as interpreted], 1992, wasn't he, and on the 24th of May, 1994, he was awarded this decoration posthumously? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know that and I don't think it's correct anyway. I'm sure his wife would know that, because she's here in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Instead of June it should say the 12th of July. The month is wrongly recorded in the transcript. Now, did you know Hazim Calagic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you don't know that he was the commander of the Independent Battalion in Voljavica from the 11th of December, 1992, through the 14th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I've already explained all the trouble and the difficulties that I had at that time, 1992/1993, and all the difficulties that I had to go through together with my family. So I've already described that. I didn't know anything about soldiers, and I couldn't really answer your questions about someone being a commander somewhere. I did not have that information, nor am I competent to answer those questions. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that, but it is important for the Defence to establish on what basis you provided certain information that had nothing to do with your family, matters that you mention in your statements that deal with and have to do with the army. So I'm just trying to find out what it was that you did know and what you didn't know. Now, I will read out the names of the commanders of this independent battalion. I will not mention the times when they were commanders. Just tell me if you knew them. Did you know Mithat Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Safet Omerovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Zajko Alic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Muharem Husic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fikret Cvrk?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Omerovic Mirzet?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, these were commanders and some of them were assistants for morale of the independent Voljavica battalion. Did you know that the Voljavica Independent Battalion existed and that it was awarded decorations and that it participated in all military operations?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Hajrudin Malagic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that he, too, was a fighter?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I describe this to you? All the people there, not only Hajrudin Malagic, who was a relative of my husband's, but all these young men who felt that they were able bodied, in the end they were forced, they had to try and protect their families when they were attacked. When we were under attack, when we were already in Srebrenica, when they had to go searching for food to bring a sack of corn from Voljavica, they went there as some sort of security. I don't know what to call them. They were just trying to protect their families, their brothers, sisters, fathers, mothers, and so on. But calling them fighters or an armed unit, I don't think that's proper, and I don't think that's what they was -- that's what they were. At least not at that time in the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Hajrudin's father Enes, is he your husband's brother?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he was a cousin?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was my father -- father's in law cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Behudin Malagic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Orhan's son?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm struggling to understand the point of this line of questions. Please move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this family was a prominent family. It was a military family, and they made a major contribution to the fighting, and this is from a chronicle of the 2nd Corps, the -- a chronicle drafted by the Muslim side. Now, I understand that this witness may not know everything, but that's what I'm trying to establish, what it is that she does know what she doesn't know. So not about what she had gone through with her family, she and her family. But she also provided some answers to general questions, and I just want to establish what it is that she does or doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you'd like, you may put your case to the witness and then move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency, but in that case I -- the Defence will be handicapped, because if the witness is unwilling to co-operate with the Defence, then we cannot really get the right answer. Now, I will move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Malagic, is it correct that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina began on the 6th of April, and five weeks after that, you left your village?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the war broke out long before I set off from my village. We, my family and I and almost everyone, we were in Voljavica almost as prisoners. At the time, I still worked in my company, but the first barricades were set up then, and we couldn't go through them. We couldn't move further. There was this disarming, and we were not allowed to get to Pobrdje. There were also barricades at Bjelovac, as far as I know, because I was told -- this was recounted by others. I never went there myself. But a week later - I don't know exactly what date it was - the work obligation was declared but only for those people who received the call-ups. Not everyone received them, and I don't know why these particular people received these call-up -- these call-ups, because not everyone did. So we stayed in our homes. But before that, as you pointed out, we could see with our own eyes, and then later we could also hear from others, and I confirm that this was correct thereby, because in Hranca I had a sister-in-law, and there was a sister-in-law and a brother in another village in the area, and they all had already experienced what we didn't in Hranca, not yet -- in Voljavica, not yet, because I know that all the houses were torched in Hranca, that Glogova was burned down completely. There was no looting, but the barns and stables were torched together with the cattle. My sister-in-law was outside working on her land when a zolja was thrown into her house. She managed to pull out her kid from the house and then to withdraw and run away, escape, together with her kid. So people were already being killed, expelled. You could see all this glare and the flames in the sky because the thing was -- the village was burning. I was told by another sister-in-law that her house had been torched. She managed to escape because she was outside of her house. So Hranca was torched. Glogova was torched. This was done by your soldiers. And that's how they came to Bratunac. On the 10th of May they set on fire the village of Mihajlevici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Please, in line 16 you said that the MUP, the police, was disarmed, but that is not in the transcript. That's on the previous page, 55. They were disarmed; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I heard it from the policeman who came to our house. I told you I don't know the date. There was this policeman, Muja Husic, who was a regular policeman in Bratunac. And also Mirsad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, is it true that you were told that there are paramilitaries in Bratunac whom they have to expel and during that time, the time it takes, the civilians must go to the stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: There were no paramilitaries. They told us as much. As far as civilians are concerned, all those villages that were torched, Mihajlevici, Redzici, and others, people from there were taken to the stadium in Bratunac. My sister-in-law told me that they had been taken to Bratunac first and from Bratunac they were taken different ways. Men were taken to the school in Karadzici and the women and children were evacuated towards Tuzla. That was happening while we were still in our village Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a Patriotic League in Bratunac? You can answer yes or no. I don't mind if it's no.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that people from Bratunac went for illegal training conducted by the MUP of Croatia and your Muslim neighbour complained about that because that was frightening the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was killed in Hranca on the occasion and how many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I do not know many of those people by name, and people were killed. You can probably hear that and check it with the witnesses from there. I know that people were killed, but how many I can't tell. I don't know. The people who did not manage to escape in time were probably killed in their own houses. I didn't know those people. I only visited occasionally my sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you can't tell us either the names or the number?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the date? Was it the 3rd or the 4th of May when that column was attacked?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date when they torched the village of Hranca. I'm not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So after that you went to Srebrenica. You say that you found Srebrenica empty except for stray dogs, and there was the stench of burning. Who set Srebrenica on fire and devastated it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Serbs did. I don't know whether they were soldiers or the inhabitants of Srebrenica. In any case, it was the Serbs, because they were the only ones in Srebrenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of troops did you find in Srebrenica when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where were the Serb residents?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: At that time while we were still at home, next door to my house, and you must know this perfectly well, there was a road through Srebrenica, Sase, Zalazje and on towards Bratunac. An enormous number of trucks and cars was passing by my house and going to Bratunac. A van would pass full of soldiers carrying weapons that were trained mostly at us. They were also sitting on the bonnets of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, with all due respect we'll get to that. Now we are in Srebrenica. You've just arrived. It's empty. There are only stray dogs.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And traces of fire. Which army did you find there when you came in?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, those first people who came down to Srebrenica, the first soldiers, didn't find anybody. It was empty. The first people to come had come from the woods where they had retreated earlier. All the real residents of Srebrenica had already fled, because you know how the others fared, all the Muslim residents, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about July 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where were your Serb neighbours? About 30 per cent of the population of Srebrenica were Serbs; right? Where were they when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, they had left of their own accord. I tried to explain this earlier. All these trucks brought people who looted everything. Every house was looted. I knew these people. They passed by my house. I don't know where they were going later. To Serbia, probably. You didn't let me explain later. A van full of soldiers would pass my house on one way, and they would all come back with each in their own car. They had Chetnik emblems, insignia, cockades. Who are these people? If they would pass again by my house a few hours later, each in their own car and all the looted property in those cars. I suppose that after the killing of Vekic all your Serb residents left Srebrenica, and Srebrenica was already empty from that time on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say they were fleeing, I see that in your first statement from 1995 you said the Serbs had started leaving, and they even carried their own dead to rebury them on the right bank of the Drina River; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your estimate, that was out of fear; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I can't say for sure why, but these things did happen. Only they know why they did it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that Naser Oric - and we have an intercept of his conversation with Mahmut Cehajic - if I tell you that he said that in early June 1992 he cleansed a few Serb villages with his army, he entered Srebrenica and cleansed it, would you accept that from that time until July 1995 Srebrenica was under his control?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, on what -- yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think it's very difficult for this witness with her experience there to comment on an intercept from Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He -- I was thinking that he was putting his case. If the witness is able to answer the question, the Chamber is fine with it. Yes, Ms. Malagic. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's leave the intercept aside. Is it a fact that from early June 1995 until July 1995 -- sorry, from early June 1992 until July 1995 Srebrenica was controlled by the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how to answer this question. When you say "the Muslim army," we probably don't define "army" in the same way, so I would be unable to answer questions of that kind. In my mind, an army is made up of people who are armed, who have logistics, who have support, who have everything. A couple of rifles, a couple of makeshift weapons, empty-handed, without anything, that's not an army. That the Muslim army attacked Srebrenica is absurd, as far as I'm concerned. How could they have been soldiers if they had no weapons? Those people that we are talking about were able-bodied men but no more than that. They were unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the Serb soldiers and the Serb authorities did not control Srebrenica between early June or even May 1992 until mid-July 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. Perhaps they did not control it strictly speaking, but in another way they did because they attacked, because they controlled our lives. We were unable to go out and get food. We had no electricity. We had no food. They controlled all of that, so how can you say they did not control Srebrenica? We could do nothing inside that town. We were like inside a camp. What kind of question is that? There's absolutely no comparison between these two sides. One of them was an army; the other one wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said those problems occurred on the 5th or 6th of May, but until that time you were left in peace, and you even said that this manager Branko had told you that you were free to work on your land in Voljavica, and he even provided diesel fuel for you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: He did that together with a neighbour who worked in the cooperative, and since that man, Branko, was the manager of that agricultural cooperative, he himself had a lot of land sown with tobacco. He was given what he needed to -- to plant it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This man Branko was a Serb who lived in Voljavica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 1995, you say that your residence captured a man by the name of Dragan and turned him over to somebody. In fact, it was the brother of this policeman, Dragan, from Pobrdje.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they must have been armed; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: You see, our young men, all of our people, stood guard. It was not a real army. They stood guard, protecting their families, their children. And that night, on the Drina River they saw boats carrying something. So they waited for them on the bank of the Drina River, and in one of the boats there was this policeman you mentioned, and they didn't need anything to get hold of this man who was carrying a load of weapons on this boat. They just took the man to the barricade in Pobrdje, and one of the men on that barricade was this Dragan. They were still holding out on these barricades against your authorities. At least they thought they would be able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On today's transcript on page 13 and earlier in this statement you said that you had arrived in this torched Srebrenica and that the Chetniks attacked Potocari on the 8th of June, and your people had only a few weapons such as hunting rifles and makeshift utensils but they still attacked these soldiers with these improvised weapons.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: That day with whatever they had, they managed somehow, but mainly with their own bodies, because everybody was either killed or seriously wounded on at that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who counted these 2.800 shells that fell on Potocari, Peciste and the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: You could hear that. I don't know. I know that shelling did not stop for a minute that day, because I was there. You couldn't go outside. You had to put a towel across your mouth. A great number of people was killed, and there were wounded, and then the people carrying the wounded would get injured as well because the shells continued falling. And they also listened to your radio communications, and from your own information, we know that on that day around 2.800 to 3.000 shells fell on Srebrenica. And the shelling never stopped and it went on from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know how much one shell costs? Five soldiers' monthly salaries. Do you think that Serbs were so generous with shells?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I know that you played your games with them. I spent five months in Potocari. It was horrible. The shells that fell only on the factory compounds, on houses. There was a house right across the river from me. From the training ground where training took place before the war to Potocari, all the way shells fell on the road, on every house in Budak; in Djogazi; in Donji Potocari, where my family also had a house; in Peciste. Every house was hit and we were able to see all of that. A shell fell on one house this minute and another house the next minute. You could watch all that. And you cannot dispute this because thousands of witnesses can tell you about it. Thousands of shells fell there only while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to where they fell and who was killed, but you say in June, Hajrudin Osmanovic was killed. Did you know these people who got killed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I knew this man Hajrudin, because his brother went to school with me. We were in the same year. That's why I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose son was he?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: The son of Mustafa Osmanovic. I think his father's name was Mustafa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know this Smajo Mehmedovic who also got killed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was my neighbour from Voljavica and also a relative, the son of Hasan Mehmedovic who worked at the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Hasan is his father; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this Resko Husic, is he Rasid's son?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about this Husein Mehmedovic, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose son was he?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I think his father's name was Smajo. This man got killed, actually went missing later as he was going to get food in Voljavica. He's been missing ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Sead Masic? Did he get killed too? Whose son was he?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Of Dzemal Masic. He hasn't been accounted for ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nedzad and Dzemal were his sons; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Nedzad lose his life then as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. But at any rate, all of these people were killed. Their father is also dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this Saban Omerovic, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew a man, an elderly man by that name, if we mean the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that he was killed then.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know whose son he was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't. I don't. He was an old man. I don't know who his father was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about this Huso Mehmedovic? Is he Husein's son?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just looking at your statement to see who lost his life. Now, in your statement you say that your legs were shaking when the shelling started again, because before that there had been a period when there was no shelling; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that when the safe haven was proclaimed, when the UN arrived, a better time came, more peaceful; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers Oric lost during that period time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Oric's soldiers went out to Serb villages every night, killed Serbs and got killed themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I note the time, so I'd like to move on to July 1995. However, perhaps that can wait for the time after the break. Tell me, please, do you know where the Serbs from the surrounding villages were, the villages around Srebrenica? Did they just stay there during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. I heard from other people that as far as those who were in Potocari were, where my brothers were, too, their neighbours took them out to Bratunac, to the Yellow Bridge, all of them from Studenac and Cumovici. As for the rest, I don't know. I don't know where they were. That was the village that was the closest to us. There weren't any other Serb villages there anyway around Potocari, I mean near Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Studenac a Serb village close to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And isn't that right that in July in Potocari you heard two soldiers talking, one of them saying, "Brother," or words to that effect, "it was so easy to liberate my village." He was from Studenac, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he was not in that village from June 1992 until July 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I see the time, so it's for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take a break for an hour, after which I expect you to come to the events of July 1995. We'll resume at 1.30, but before doing that, can I hear from you? I think you can make your submission in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, you had asked about the investigator Tomasz Blaszczyk, and my -- we will have four investigators. He will be the first, testifying today. His testimony is going to regard the 360 QuickTime presentation of the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. I will note that before he testifies, the technicians will need 20 minutes to upload the equipment for the presentation. He will be followed by Investigator Ruez who will be talking about all the crime sites. The other two investigators in the case will testify later in the case, and that is both Dusan Janc and Dean Manning. They will be talking about the forensics and Janc will be specifically talking about the DNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And my question was specifically --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And your question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The content of Mr. Blaszczyk's evidence with respect to updating and discussing the report of Mr. Dean Manning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that appears to be incorrect. At this point he is talking about the road between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac, and he will be talking about the Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that the Chamber is not going to give me less time than that the -- than the examination-in-chief took. So I should have all of today and tomorrow as well. That's according to 92 ter. The Prosecution spent more than two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you talking about your cross-examination of Madam Malagic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because Blaszczyk has been announced for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You waste -- you spent already an hour on the issues the relevance of which we doubt. You have exactly a bit more than half an hour, a bit -- I think you may have 35 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was corrected. You will have 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say a word? If that is unimportant, why is the Prosecution asking for information from 1992 through this witness? What matters to the Prosecution matters to the Defence as well. Secondly, the Prosecution spent more than two hours, and I am supposed to spend an hour and a half, and I have 92 ter as well. The entire Krstic transcript. So could I please be given all of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I was advised that the Prosecution spent one hour and 35 minutes, and you will have exactly 45 minutes this session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency [In English] But usually with 92 ter, the Defence should have more than the Prosecution because I have the whole transcript from Krstic to deal, let alone the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber is of the opinion that one and a half hours is more than sufficient for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I've made this observation before, Dr. Karadzic, and it's just as true now as it was then: You should really be concentrating on the matters which are contained within the indictment. This isn't an exercise in historical revaluation or an attempt to look at every fact and determine every fact. There are obviously facts which go to the indictment and thus bring into play elements of the law which we have to apply, and by taking a careful look at the indictment and taking advice certainly from Mr. Robinson, it's certainly my view, and I suspect the view of my colleagues that you could focus far more accurately on the facts that are important than you often do, and certainly raising matters which are more appropriate to the issue of tu quoque really doesn't help anybody and do not assist in the determination of this indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. But I have a feeling that what the Prosecution is presenting has a purpose, an objective, and I'll trying to get to the bottom of that, but I'll try to follow your instructions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Malagic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not giving you instructions. I'm giving you advice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Advice, right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the transcript when you testified in General Krstic's trial, on page 1942, you said that your people during the first shelling wanted to leave Srebrenica because they were afraid that the Serbs would take revenge; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, on that page, 1942, you said -- I'm now going to read this out in English so that the interpretation is better. "[In English] We were all on our way to Potocari and on the road there were very many people there, and when the Serb soldiers began to shell the town and then they simply wanted to take revenge. People didn't know where to turn, where to go." [Interpretation] Was that the assessment, that the Serbs would take revenge?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, we knew that things didn't look good for us. As soon as the shelling started -- I mean, we had already experienced that before at the beginning of the war, and we knew as soon as the shelling started, when they started shelling people in town itself, as I've already described, everybody thought that it was better to get out as soon as possible, because of course, if one were to get into their hands, I mean we'd probably end up the way other people did in the beginning of the war. What else could we expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know approximately what it was that the Serbs wanted to take their revenge for?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. We did not think that they had any major reason for that. In my view, now this is my personal view, if anyone had a reason for revenge, we were such a long-suffering people. Perhaps we had more reason if, I'm saying if, we were to take revenge on anyone. Long-suffering, exhausted. I mean, all the suffering I went through over those three years. They really had no reason for that. Now, what their objectives were, well, we knew that nothing good would come out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that your father-in-law said, "Ah, now we're done in," when he saw this acquaintance of his with whom he was not on very good terms; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So are you trying to say that it was possible for some of these individuals to settle their own accounts and to take revenge for things that happened long ago?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Knowing that man, the one that I mentioned - I knew him, too - he was always -- well, how do I put this? Everything he said was supposed to be some kind of a joke, but there was always this nationalist drift even when he made these jokes, and he had conflicts not only with my father-in-law but also with other people who were ethnic Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he the only person of this kind or were there other people who took advantage of the situation in order to settle their own personal accounts?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. In Potocari at that point in time I didn't really see any other acquaintances. I saw Serb soldiers. I saw ethnic Serbs, but I didn't see people I knew when we crossed this UNPROFOR barricade, and before that there were some who were simply watching what was going on. As I said, they walked among the people, but they did not do anything, I mean anything abnormal or bad or whatever. Now, what happened later to these people, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a microphone on somewhere because I hear more than I would like to. I hear interpretation. [In English] Somewhere a speaker, I suppose, Your Honour, is on. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said today during the examination-in-chief and also in your statements that the people moved and tried to go towards the UN on the 10th of June, and you arrived at this first compound, UN compound; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Srebrenica had not fallen by that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, not yet, but the UNPROFOR point was moved. It was at Ljubistivica [phoen], or whatever it was called, where the UNPROFOR soldiers were. They were already -- they already moved from there up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this your own decision or was this something that was suggested by someone in authority, that this would be a good course to follow?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to move towards Srebrenica? What do you mean? I'm not sure what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. To move and head for the UN compound on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, we were at the elementary school, and we saw that a large number of people had already started moving towards Srebrenica from all those areas, Ucina Basta, Pekara [phoen], Jadar itself. All of those people from those areas had already gone to Srebrenica and they were all moving towards the UNPROFOR compound. It was a movement of the population. It wasn't organised or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the same thing happened again on the 11th, correct, again before the Serbs arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 11th, in the morning, I can't recall exactly what time it was, we were still in the building, when my brother left we saw these columns of people moving again because they had already come back, and then they literally said, "Well, they returned sooner than we thought they would. Do you want us all to be captured?" So they said that the Serbs had already come to the Srebrenica MUP. So they had already been in Srebrenica when I left the building and moved towards the UNPROFOR compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you also say that at this point some trucks appeared. You say this on page 1944. UNPROFOR trucks appeared. They were full of people, and people used this mode of transportation to move towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know if people used this. They did not take anyone from the compound. Everybody had to get down. I assume, and I don't know if this information is correct, because I saw that my son was there. I assumed that they had returned them and they wanted to -- they asked for the people from the hospital to be evacuated. So they were there on the truck, and I saw this because the tarp was torn and it was -- it wasn't covering the truck, so that's when I saw him there and also this friend of his, and they were trying to evacuate the wounded persons. I don't know what happened with the others. They probably walked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. "[In English] Not far from Potocari, about a kilometre, I --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you start your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here's what you say on page 1944: "[In English] Not far from Potocari, about a kilometre, I'm not quite sure, a lot of people overtook us and two UNPROFOR trucks also arrived, caught up with us, and they were crammed with people." [Interpretation] And then on page 1946 you say, on line 9, that people boarded these trucks, UNPROFOR trucks, and a number of people left on foot, whereas the others went on trucks and were taken to the UNPROFOR compound; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. People were trying to get on these trucks while we were originally in the compound in Srebrenica. They thought they could go that way. However, when we set off on foot, when we were told that we should go to Potocari, all those people had to get off those trucks. They weren't taken on the trucks from there. So then we all walked in a column towards Potocari on foot. Then on -- halfway there, I'm not sure exactly where we were, two of those trucks overtook us, and I only saw -- on one of these trucks where the tarp was torn, I saw my son and this other boy, his friend, his friend from Srebrenica. I saw the two of them. At least that was my assumption, because I know that as we were leaving, I know that they were pleading with these guys to let them evacuate the wounded people, and I assume that maybe that's what they did. And that's my assumption again, that that's how he arrived to the Potocari compound, the UN Potocari compound, where he got off and then that's the last time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there was shooting, that there were a lot of shells. You said that there was shooting opened on a line of people waiting for the water. When was and who was it who was killed in the waterline in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, there were so many thousands of people in Srebrenica in these waterlines. How do you imagine that I could tell you who of these people were killed? Do you understand that entire -- I don't know who was killed. There were entire cemeteries, new cemeteries sprang up because so many were killed. There were people getting killed everywhere throughout the town, not just in one particular area, not in waterlines. There were people dying everywhere. Now, who these people were, how could I tell? I really can't tell you. I can't even tell you how many of them were killed, but believe me, there were so many people dead in Srebrenica. Nobody could keep count --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you remember that other than the shell that landed on the football pitch during a football match, do you recall any other mass killing of that sort in Srebrenica, in a line of some sort, between the time when Srebrenica was provide a protected area and July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Sir, in those days when I was there, a shell did land. I can't recall what date it was, but there were people who had come from Cerska and Konjevic Polje and on that occasion a shell landed there and a woman and two children got killed. There were a lot of people there coming from other towns, and there were three people killed at one spot at one time there. The house in which we lived at the time, when this shell exploded, all the glass on the windows broke. There wasn't only one shell. There were shells falling all the time, so it's hard to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, there were some 700 to 800 days, almost a thousand days, between the time when the area was declared a protected area and June 1995. When was it that that shell landed where you said that your -- you -- your legs gave way under you and that you were so scared because there hadn't been many before the?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, this was all in the first war year when all this was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you were aware -- you knew that in July 1996 -- my apologies. I'm pressed for time. That's why I'm rushing. So you did know that the Serbs were not really shelling and not aiming to kill, that they were shelling -- that the shells were falling on the side of the road, and their intention was different, not to kill; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in my view, as we were on our way to Potocari then, it was really just their attempt to intimidate people, because there were shells falling on the side, but -- and some people were hit by shrapnel, but it was hard to actually keep your head on your shoulders because there were many children there. They were terrified and everybody was trying to peach Potocari as soon as they could. They were moving very fast, we were moving very fast. There were elderly people in the column as well, women and children, and of course they lagged behind a bit, behind the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 1946 you say that UNPROFOR recommended that you move towards Potocari and that you heard planes overhead. And then on the next page you say that the shells were falling on either side of the road. And then on the next page, 1947, you talk about what you've just mentioned here, that you thought that these shells were intended to intimidate. Now, do you agree with the opinion of others whom we've heard here that these shells were meant to actually make people stick to the road, that they were not supposed to veer away, veer off from the road, that they should stay on the road?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, on the other side of Potocari there were meadows, other people's land, and you couldn't really take any other way, any other road. There was no need to -- to go any other way other than the road that we were already walking on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned today, I believe, and then on page 1949 you said that many shells landed on the separation line, the line separating the Serb and the Muslim armies; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the night of the 11th going on the 12th, you said that it was rather calm; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then on the 12th of July, you saw Serbian soldiers for the first time. That was the first time that they actually came up to you, that they established contact with you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You describe on page 1950 that no one was sure where to go. Everyone was wondering which way to go. Before this, you decided as a family that civilians, you, your father-in-law, and the youngest child, should join the civilians and head for Potocari; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this something that was suggested by someone else or was this purely your own decision?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: It was my decision, our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this decision coincide with the decisions that most other people decide to take?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was it who decided that able-bodied men should head towards Susnjari -- toward Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know that there was any official decision. As for my men, and I'm speaking on their behalf, they simply decided to head that way. Just like in 1992, we did not trust the Serbs to surrender to them. So the same feeling prevailed, and they decided to try and head for Susnjari and then reach the so-called free territory that way, to try to break through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I would like to ask you about, you say that they -- well, they could go in four different directions. How was it that 15 -- 13.000 to 15.000 people decided to go in this one particular direction to Susnjari? How could that be?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I know that most people who were there who were from Cerska and Konjevic Polje, there were even some people from Zvornik municipality, I believe that they were familiar with this road. Simply that was the reason. Some people decided to go back to Zepa. So I really don't know how it was that they decided to go that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that about 1.000 Oric's men crossed the Drina by way of Zepa and crossed into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I did hear that some people managed to cross over into Serbia, but who they were and whether they were fighters or not, I don't know. I don't know if they were civilians or soldiers. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that some houses that were uninhabitable and some other buildings, that there were haystacks, and as the Serb army was coming downhill, down the slope, that they were torching everything before them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, where did these haystacks come from? How -- how did that happen to be there? Was someone actually cutting grass?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, people lived there, and these people were people who lived there and were just tilling their soil, working their land.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the hay was meant for cattle; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the houses that you mentioned, did anyone explain to you that when an army goes through a certain area, they cannot leave any buildings behind them because there might be someone hidden in those buildings who could then shoot at their backs?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, how could anyone explain anything like that to us? We didn't know what we were doing. Why would anyone be explaining anything? All we could see was that they were setting everything on fire, and then when arrived -- when they arrived there, then we realised who they were. Of course, "we" meaning all of our people who were all over the place there on the plateau, around some factory and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned today that there was a lot of shooting into the air. They were celebrating something, celebratory shooting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On line 13, page 1951, you speak about this, and then you say that the Serb soldiers then mixed in or came and joined you, the population, the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They came. They went from group to group from us and they asked us, you know, about things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they were asking you about how you were doing, who -- your names and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned, they asked about things such as where our sons were, where our husbands were, and stuff like that. Personally, no one addressed me. No one asked me anything or asked for any names or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 1952, you say that they were looking for children. Some gave chocolate bars and chewing gum to children. The children were very hungry for these things, and they accepted gladly; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And on the next page, 1953, you say, and you've also repeated that on pages 38 and 39, that on several occasions they called out people to interrogate them. They called out one person once, twice, and a third time. That person did not come back.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What could they have learned about that person in the meantime? Why didn't they take them out straight away?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Some people did not return after the first time they were taken out, and a couple of other people who were interrogated once or twice did not return on the third time. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 1953, you say you saw an UNPROFOR soldier tied to a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you maybe imagine that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking, because nobody ever reported that we had tied an UNPROFOR soldier to his vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: When we went out to get some water, there was an UNPROFOR vehicle in the street, and there was a soldier lying on his back with his arms outstretched and tied behind his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In some of your statements you said - and I hope this was a slip of the tongue - that Serbs had taken out several hundred young women. They separated them from the others. Nobody ever reported about that to us. Did somebody tell you that or did you see them separating young women?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I saw these young women being separated from the others and taken away towards houses to the right of Srebrenica, towards, for instance, the house of Hasan Malic and his neighbours, the houses lying below my brother's house, which was devastated at the time. They took them to those houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't object to the question, but Mr. Karadzic mentioned statements. As I understand, there's only one statement, so if he's speaking about there being more than one, I would just appreciate a cite.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two transcripts of this witness's testimony, in Tolimir and in Krstic, and also a statement, a written statement, from 1995. I can find a reference later. I think this passage comes from the 1995 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that some people taunted you, mentioning Alija and asking you why you did not listen to Babo, your daddy.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: That's the man who cursed our Balija mother, and saying that if we had listened to Babo, that is to say, Alija, the things that were happening would not be happening to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree -- and I'm saying this because the Chamber does not know who Babo is, do you know that Babo is a Muslim leader who overwhelmingly won the elections in 1992 but is of a different political affiliation than Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that sort of question, Mr. Karadzic, which politician belonged to what party and who got more votes. I was not involved in that, and I don't know what would have happened if we had listened to this one or that one. I'm an ordinary woman who survived what she has survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do know that it is a Muslim leader whom the Serbs preferred over Alija, and these Serbs were telling you if you had listened to Babo, then these things would not be happening. You know he's a Muslim leader; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 1959 and 1958, you say that moaning could be heard from people who were being tortured in the white house or wherever it was they were interrogated. How is it possible that nobody from the UNPROFOR reported about that, although all 150 of them were there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: That's rubbish, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It was a classic example of asking somebody what's in a third party's mind, Dr. Karadzic. If the Prosecution did that, you'd be the first to object.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm making an introduction to what the UNPROFOR told them. On page 1959, UNPROFOR said -- sorry. Page 58, line 23: "[In English] We wanted to know what would happen to the people, to the men whose families were screaming, but they would," next page, "they would simply answer that a member of their families must have gone mad or something like that and they told us not to be afraid and that it was nothing really."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So UNPROFOR did not see that anybody was being tortured, and they thought the families were going crazy and perhaps exaggerating.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: You know better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll let it go because she already started her answer. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I still object on the same grounds. And secondly, Mr. Karadzic has not read this entire passage, because these are soldiers of which she was -- were actually Serb soldiers that she said were wearing UNPROFOR uniforms. So they're not Dutch soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would you like to hear again "rubbish" from the witness? Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that it was only your assumption, and you supposed that somebody had committed suicide. How many people committed suicide?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Some people committed suicide. There was one man I saw with my own eyes that night who hanged himself when he saw what was going on. After midnight nobody was sleeping. He hanged himself in the compound of the Zinc factory. I know that man. He was a relative of mine, Hamdije Smajlovic. From the accounts of his family, his wife, who was going back with us, their house was close to mine, I know that her husband also hanged himself, and there were many other people who did not know what to do or where to go and decided to take their own lives. All the people your Serb soldiers took away the evening of the 12th, not a single shot could be heard. Only screams and moans could be heard. And it was not the white house. There were two houses next to the Zinc factory. Some people were taken there that night. There were screams, awful screams and cries. You couldn't really determine where they were coming from. Also from the compound of the transport company. All this screaming was coming from everywhere, like in a horror film. The night was filled with it. People could not understand what was going on, but the families around us all lost family members, men who were taken out that night and never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, with all due respect. On page 1958 and 59, the witness assumed those were Serbian soldiers because they knew the Serbian language, but there is no other proof that they were Serbian soldiers. I'm telling you, madam, that it's impossible that Serbian soldiers would be wearing UNPROFOR uniforms in front of UNPROFOR troops. So you decided that they were Serbian only because they were speaking Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: No. I saw one soldier when he was taking his T-shirt off and giving it to another soldier. And we had spent a lot of time with Dutch troops in Srebrenica before that. Not a single one of them knew our language that well. On the 13th, in the morning, when we were asking them what to do and where to go, they were smiling so happily. You know who can smile like that? Somebody who achieved their goal. They spoke Serbian so perfectly there's no chance they were Dutch. Not a single Dutch soldier could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You never mentioned that soldier who was taking his T-shirt off before.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I could write a novel if I were to mention everything that happened during those years and that -- these days in Potocari. There are things coming back all the time. And people who were grown up, who had moved among these soldiers during those years knew perfectly well not a single Dutch soldier spoke Serbian so well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned for the first time in this testimony, on page 1969, that young women were separated from the others and taken away. They took daughters and young girls. I'm giving this reference for the benefit of the other participants in the trial. And you now say that some people hanged themselves. You know one of them. You knew one of them, Hamdije Smajlovic. How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: He was a cousin, and before the war he worked in the Zinc factory, in the servicing shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What's his father's name?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Demir Smajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Kiram Smajlovic? Did he hang himself too?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I knew the man, but I didn't see him hang himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you told -- I'll tell you now on which page, 1960. My next-door neighbour -- I'll read in English: [Overlapping speakers] ... "[In English] A next-door neighbour of mine, she had a house in the vicinity of the factory. They were going home to get some food and she told me that on the way she had seen two other persons, two of our neighbours, who had hanged themselves. Kiram Smajic and Fehim Hasanovic." [Interpretation] Right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know this man Kiram?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know his father's name?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Nazif Smajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nazif or Kemal?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Nazif.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to those whom you later learned to be dead or to have committed suicide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I don't think the next witness can begin. It takes 20 minutes only to set up the courtroom, so just because of the circumstances you could give me a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have exactly 15 minutes conclude your evidence -- cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic. Sorry, five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 1983, you stated, line 16: "[In English] I can corroborate it by fresh examples from my family. My father-in-law Omer Malagic, born in 1926, his three sons, one of whom was my husband Salko Malagic, born 1948. His two brothers Osman Malagic, Dzafer Malagic, his three grandsons, these are my two sons, Elvir Malagic born in 1973, Admir Malagic born in 1979, and my brother-in-law Samir Malagic." [Interpretation] They're all dead; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When were they killed, respectively?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: My father-in-law, as I said before, Omer Malagic; my husband Salko Malagic; Samir Malagic, and the others all were killed at the time Srebrenica fell, whereas my brother-in-law Osman Malagic was killed in Srebrenica sometime in June. I don't know the date. Whereas Dzafer Malagic was killed in December 1992. Also while searching for food, he was killed by an air-bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And those who were killed in July, where were they killed and how? They attempted a breakthrough, all of them except your father-in-law; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: As I said before, when I went to identify the bodies in Tuzla, we had all received papers beforehand and I presented them to the OTP, and there are protocols listing the place where they were killed and the grave where they were found. The locations were Zvornicka, Kamenica, where the executions took place. Regarding my son, the cause of death is indicated as possible entry and exit wound in the chest. And for my husband the cause of death is not determined because the bones were collected from several sites. It was not a complete skeleton, and the doctor could not establish the cause of death, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of certificate did you obtain regarding these victims? How were they qualified in the certificates?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive certificates for them as what, casualties, civilian victims, or combatants? It's indicated on the certificate.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: My husband is listed as combatant, and children, victims of war, casualties of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 1991, you repeated that a thousand women did not return from Potocari, and 106 -- and 650 children didn't. Do you stand by that claim that the Serbs kept a thousand women and 650 children?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: That doesn't mean that the Serbs kept them. I heard various stories, and one man told me that his entire family that boarded a truck in Potocari did not arrive at Tuzla. Where those people ended up is a matter for speculation. Some women were killed too. Where they were killed and how they met their death, I don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is written in this 92 ter notification, that out of all the men some were separated by Serb soldiers, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Please put a pause before you start answering the question, Ms. Malagic. Could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic. That may be -- this should be the last question from you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just ask one final question? Can this be the penultimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here in the notification, 92 ter notification, the Prosecutor claims that you were separated from your sons and your husband by Serb soldiers. That's not quite correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, literally speaking, perhaps you could claim that it's not correct, but in fact it is correct. We were separated by Serb soldiers. I mean, they weren't literally there at that spot and then separating us. We were -- rather, we were forced to separate, but we separated because of the Serb soldiers, because of the shelling, because of trying not to fall in their hands. So we were separated at -- on the outskirts of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question: We mentioned today a large number of people who were killed in 1992, and also some people who committed suicide, as well as those who went missing while they were trying a breakthrough towards Tuzla. Are all those names etched in on the memorial in Srebrenica, the monument, the memorial site there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: All the names, all of those people who were killed when Srebrenica fell, or killed, those who were trying to break through and so on, but all of those who were killed before that time, earlier on, their names are not on this memorial monument. They are -- they were buried in other locations, in other areas. So only those who were killed in Potocari or Srebrenica they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if I tell you that they're on lists, on DNA-identification lists, including the suicides, if I told you that they were on the 1992 list of -- would -- and that's not correct, what would you say to that? Where did these other people get killed -- get buried?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the Kazani cemetery, the Potocari cemetery, some mass cemeteries where a number of people were buried at the same time, especially during intense shelling. In other words, in all the areas around Srebrenica when there was a cemetery already or there was free space, anyway, they established cemeteries and buried people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, where are those cemeteries now?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, they're still in Srebrenica, in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question: The Prosecutor tried to link this with something that you saw in Sandici. When was this? When did this happen? What date and at what time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: Well, this was on the 13th of July. I was on the bus at the time. Around -- in the early afternoon, around 1.00 or 2.00 p.m. like now. I'm not quite sure, because I didn't have a watch. So I'm not sure about the time, but the sun was already high on the sky.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you know that on the night of the 12 -- between the 12th and the 13th there were no Serb soldiers in Potocari, and you said that that night was horrible.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA MALAGIC
utterances.text: The 12th, on the 13th of July? Sir, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not have enough time to complete fully my questioning. And that the Defence should be allotted the same amount of time as the Prosecution in the 92 ter situation, that's really a novelty too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I would like you to read back the transcript of today and find out what kind of questions you were asking to the witness for the first hour. Ms. West, would you like to have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, may I just add one final word. May I say something, and this has to do with my questions at the beginning of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. Ms. Malagic, that concludes your evidence in this case. On behalf of my colleagues and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Malagic, on behalf of the Defence, and I hope you hold no grudge against us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who will lead the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that we need 15 minutes to prepare for the next witness, but still there's a point, but it's worth it to continue even if it's for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break for 15 minutes and resume at quarter to 3.00. --- Break taken at 2.28 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Blaszczyk. My apologies for pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are appearing again for a second time, but for clarity, I would prefer you to take the solemn declaration again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. Before I begin, Your Honours, may I raise one matter briefly which I've discussed with my friend Mr. Robinson, and that is I would ask that the OTP be allowed to have contact and speak with Mr. Blaszczyk while he is testifying solely on the issue of scheduling of other witnesses because he sometimes assists us and the people doing the scheduling with witness phone numbers and addresses and things like that, and my friend does not have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It is granted, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As you know, today for a short time and tomorrow we're going to discuss an exhibit you've created, 65 ter 03931, and we may bring that up in e-court now, which we call the Petrovic Video Road Book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I believe you should all have a copy, a hard copy, and I've passed it out to Mr. Karadzic and to Mr. Harvey as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
